<meta>continues from previous page: Sāriputta's "lion's roar", in which he answers a charge of having offended a fellow monk by describing the state of his own mind through a series of similes</meta>
<header>Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.</header>

Just as, venerable sir, a duster¹ wipes up what is clean and wipes up what is unclean, wipes up excrement², wipes up urine³, wipes up spittle⁴, wipes up pus⁵ ⁶, wipes up blood, and yet that duster is not troubled, ashamed or disgusted by it: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a duster, vast, exalted, measureless⁷, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.

Just as, venerable sir, an outcaste boy⁸ or an outcaste girl⁹, bowl in hand¹⁰ and dressed in rags¹¹, enters a village or a town with a humble mind already set up: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste boy¹², vast, exalted, measureless⁷, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.
<note>The <term>caṇḍāla</term> <gloss>outcaste</gloss> was the lowest group in Indian society, expected to show deference on entering a settlement.</note>

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with its horns cut off, gentle¹³, well tamed and well trained¹⁴, wandering from street to street¹⁵ and from crossroads to crossroads, harms no one at all, whether with foot or with horn: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted⁷, measureless, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.

Just as, venerable sir, a woman or a man, young¹⁶, youthful³, fond of adornment¹⁷, having bathed the head³ ¹⁸, by the carcass of a snake or

---

¹ T., M₆ and M. read puñjati; S. reads muñcati throughout.
² omitted by M., Ph., T. and S. ³ omitted by M., Ph. and S.
⁴ omitted by M., Ph., M₆ and S. ⁵ omitted by T.
⁶ omitted by M., Ph., M₆ and S. ⁷ M₆ and M. abbreviate: pe ‖ āsajja <note>"and so on" up to āsajja</note>.
⁸ T. reads ºkumāro. ⁹ T. reads ºkumārī. ¹⁰ Ph. reads kaḷoviº.
¹¹ M₆ reads nantakaº; T., M₆ and M. read ºvāsini.
¹² M. reads caṇḍālakumārakacaṇḍālakumārikaº <gloss>like an outcaste boy or outcaste girl</gloss>.
¹³ M. and S. read surato. ¹⁴ S. reads ºsikkhito <gloss>well disciplined</gloss>.
¹⁵ T., M₆ and M. read rathiyā. ¹⁶ omitted by M. and Ph.
¹⁷ T. reads maṇḍanaº. ¹⁸ omitted by S.

<summary>In this part of Sāriputta's lion's roar from the Book of Nines of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, he compares his mind to a duster that wipes up filth without disgust, to a humble outcaste child, and to a dehorned, gentle bull, each time insisting that only a monk without mindfulness of the body would offend a fellow monk and leave without apology. The page breaks off in the middle of a further simile.</summary>
